strengths: Strong empirical results with comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating clear gains on spatial reasoning tasks, particularly for distance/size/direction estimation
Valuable dataset contributions including 200K curated QA pairs and 138.6K-pair VSTemporalI-Bench addressing an important evaluation gap for temporal reasoning
Practical and scalable approach that eliminates dependency on depth sensors or pre-built 3D maps by leveraging monocular video, addressing real limitations of prior work
Well-executed integration of 3D reconstruction with efficient architectural design (frozen encoders, LoRA fine-tuning) enabling practical deployment
Thorough experimental validation with clear ablations (Table 3) showing contributions of geometric and camera tokens across diverse baselines
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty—core contribution is integrating existing components (CUT3R, cross-attention, LLM) via standard fusion mechanisms rather than novel methodology. The cross-attention fusion (Eq. 2) is straightforward, lacking conceptual innovation expected for top-tier venues

Fundamental reconstruction quality limitations not addressed: paper acknowledges monocular reconstruction underperforms sensor-derived depth for fine-grained tasks (object size: 69.15 vs 70.82 baseline), but provides no mitigation strategy

Critical evaluation gaps: VSTemporalI-Bench limited to static scenes (camera-only motion, no object motion explicitly deferred to future work), potential train/test contamination from using same 3 datasets for both training and evaluation, and evaluation restricted to indoor scenes without diversity

Missing comparisons with other 3D-aware VLMs (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT, 3D-LLaVA-Instruct, LLaVA-3D)—only compares against general video LLMs, making it impossible to assess contribution relative to competing 3D-aware approaches

Automated data generation quality not validated: deterministic QA generation from scene graphs offers limited diversity, no human evaluation of quality, and unexplored risk of spurious correlations between generation logic and model behavior

Incomplete technical justification: no ablation on LoRA rank (128), training for only 1 epoch without convergence analysis, camera token encoding poorly explained, and design choices (cross-attention vs. alternatives) lack comparison
Computational costs and practical deployment implications not discussed—CUT3R's dense transformer operations likely add inference overhead not quantified or analyzed
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, external dependency on CUT3R, and many critical details relegated to appendix

strengths: Addresses a practical limitation: proposes a scalable alternative to depth sensors and pre-built 3D maps for spatial reasoning in VLMs, working directly from monocular video
Comprehensive benchmark contribution: introduces VSTemporalI-Bench with 138.6K QA pairs to evaluate an underexplored aspect (temporal spatial reasoning)
Strong empirical results: ranks 1st among 7B open-source models on VSI-Bench and shows consistent performance across multiple benchmarks
Substantial data curation effort: curated 200K+ training QA pairs through automated pipeline from existing 3D datasets
Thorough ablation studies: clearly demonstrates individual contributions of geometry tokens (↓4.6 rel. dist) and camera tokens (↓1.7 rel. dir)
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and training configuration provided in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core approach is primarily an engineering integration of off-the-shelf components (frozen CUT3R, CLIP ViT, LLaVA-Video) connected via standard cross-attention fusion. The fusion mechanism (concatenate tokens → cross-attention → MLP) lacks technical innovation

Misleading framing on '3D reconstruction': the paper claims 'instruction-aligned 3D reconstruction' but CUT3R is frozen during training. VLM-3R learns to use reconstruction outputs, not to reconstruct—the framing obscures this dependence
Heavy reliance on pre-trained 3D model: all 3D understanding comes from CUT3R, raising questions about what VLM-3R actually learns. Computational overhead and failure modes of CUT3R are not analyzed

New benchmark limitations: VSTemporalI-Bench is authored by the submission team with no independent validation. All temporal tasks assume static scenes with camera motion only (acknowledged as future work). Auto-generated QA pairs may exhibit systematic biases not present in manually-annotated data

Incomplete evaluation: (1) Limited to indoor scenes from 3 datasets (ScanNet, ARKitScenes); (2) No comparison with other recent 3D-aware VLMs like ROSS3D or newer 3D-LLaVA variants; (3) No runtime/computational cost analysis despite end-to-end processing; (4) Still ranks behind proprietary models (Gemini-1.5 Pro is rank 1 on VSI-Bench); (5) Underperforms on object size estimation (69.15 vs 70.82 baseline), suggesting reconstruction quality doesn't uniformly help

Scalability claims not substantiated: 200K pairs from existing datasets is not exceptional. Route planning (only 4,225 pairs) comes from simulation, and all data depends on having access to 3D scene datasets. The 'minimal cost' claim lacks supporting evidence
Training details raise concerns: stopped after 1 epoch (of 5 planned) without explanation or convergence analysis. No learning curves shown. Unclear why early stopping occurred

Generalization not demonstrated: (1) No outdoor scenes; (2) No unconstrained real-world video; (3) No failure case analysis; (4) No ablation on architecture choices (why this fusion design? why 432×432 resolution?); (5) No analysis of how reconstruction noise/errors propagate to reasoning tasks

Architectural design choices under-justified: the paper lacks ablation on fusion mechanisms (e.g., why cross-attention vs. additive fusion?), token concatenation strategy, or resolution trade-offs. Skip connection is mentioned but not detailed or ablated

Presentation issues: (1) Figure 1 duplicated on consecutive pages; (2) Overclaimed novelty ('first 3D vision-language framework...from monocular RGB video' while relying on frozen CUT3R); (3) 'End-to-end' is misleading when spatial encoder is frozen; (4) Insufficient qualitative analysis—no visualizations of learned representations, attention patterns, or error cases

strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical benefits: eliminates dependency on depth sensors or pre-built 3D maps, making spatial reasoning scalable to monocular video
Thoughtful system design: Spatial-Visual-View Fusion elegantly integrates 3D geometry tokens, camera view tokens, and 2D features via principled cross-attention mechanism

Comprehensive experimental validation with strong results: ranks 1st among 7B models on VSI-Bench (60.9 vs 40.9 for LLaVA-72B), outperforming some 72B and proprietary models; particularly strong on geometry-dependent tasks

Valuable dataset contributions: 200K+ curated spatial QA pairs with systematic automated generation pipeline, plus new VSTemporalI-Bench with 138.6K pairs addressing gap in temporal reasoning evaluation
Convincing ablation studies clearly demonstrating individual component contributions (geometry tokens, camera tokens) with proper baselines
Strong temporal reasoning performance: demonstrates effectiveness in understanding camera dynamics and object relationships (58.8 vs 44.0 on VSTemporalI-Bench)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components are off-the-shelf (CUT3R frozen, standard cross-attention, LoRA fine-tuning); contribution is primarily system integration and data curation rather than methodological innovation

Evaluation scope limitations: VSTemporalI-Bench covers only static scenes with camera movement, no independent object motion; all training/test data from same sources (indoor ScanNet/ARKitScenes); generalization to outdoor scenes and dynamic objects unexplored

Fair comparison concerns: VLM-3R trained on 200K additional specialized QA pairs while baselines use standard data; unclear how much improvement is from architecture vs. additional curated training; limited ablation comparing baseline fine-tuned on same QA data

Reconstruction quality limitations inadequately addressed: Object Size task underperformance (69.15 vs 70.82) reveals weakness; no investigation of failure modes (lighting, occlusions, texture-less regions) or robustness; frozen CUT3R prevents exploration of fine-tuning benefits

Limited failure case analysis and generalization: minimal discussion of when/why VLM-3R fails; Appearance Order notably weak (40.1); no error analysis by scene complexity or spatial configuration; lack of attention visualizations

Incomplete computational analysis: inference time not reported; training convergence unspecified; no computational cost comparison with baselines; CUT3R's multi-frame processing overhead not discussed

Dataset quality concerns: 200K QA pairs automatically generated from metadata without human validation or quality control; potential distribution shift between synthetic training QA and real spatial reasoning tasks not assessed

Limited analysis of learned representations: minimal insight into what fusion mechanism learns; unclear whether geometry tokens genuinely capture spatial information or are bypassed; no visualization of 3D vs 2D feature importance

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Spatial reasoning from monocular video without depth sensors addresses a genuine scalability challenge in deploying spatial AI systems.

Thoughtful architectural design: The use of implicit 3D tokens from CUT3R avoids explicit point cloud sparsity issues, and Spatial-Visual-View Fusion via cross-attention provides clean integration with evidence supporting CUT3R over VGGT (Table D).
Comprehensive data curation pipeline: Systematic generation of 207K+ QA pairs using structured spatio-temporal scene graphs with careful train/test split adherence demonstrates rigor.

Valuable benchmark contribution: VSTI-Bench (138.6K QA pairs) addresses a gap in temporal reasoning evaluation with thoughtful task design covering camera dynamics, camera-object interactions, and object relations.

Extensive experimental validation: Evaluation across VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, Video-MME, and OpenEQA with comprehensive ablations (spatial tokens, view tokens, fusion strategies, geometry encoders) and data mixing analysis.

Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements on VSI-Bench (60.9% overall, +3.2pp over base), leading performance on VSTI-Bench (58.8%), and competitive results on 3D QA benchmarks using only monocular video.
Reproducibility support: Detailed hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, preprocessing pipelines, and training configurations provided in supplementary materials enable reproduction efforts.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution combines existing components (pre-trained CUT3R, standard cross-attention, LLaVA-NeXT-Video architecture, LoRA fine-tuning) rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques. Novelty lies primarily in effective integration.

Insufficient data vs. architecture ablation: No comparison of 2D-only LLaVA with 200K spatial QA pairs; no training curves or data scaling analysis. Unclear whether improvements stem from superior training data rather than architectural design, which is critical for understanding true contribution.

Frozen encoder design unjustified: Both visual and spatial encoders are frozen during training with no ablation or justification provided. End-to-end fine-tuning could potentially yield better results but remains unexplored.

Narrow evaluation domain: Training and evaluation restricted to indoor, static 3D scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes). VSTI-Bench also limited to static scenes with purely camera-driven motion. No evaluation on outdoor scenes, dynamic objects, or extreme conditions limits generalizability claims.

Incomplete 3D reconstruction impact analysis: Object Size accuracy lower (69.2% vs. 70.8%), attributed vaguely to 'monocular 3D reconstruction quality.' No analysis of how CUT3R errors propagate to reasoning tasks, failure cases, or how reconstruction quality varies across scene types.

General-to-spatial task trade-off under-addressed: Video-MME performance drops from 62.7% (base) to 59.9% (spatial-only); data mixing partially recovers this (62.1%) but trade-off deserves deeper discussion regarding domain specialization costs.

Missing computational analysis: No inference speed, computational cost comparisons, or memory requirement quantification. CUT3R processing overhead not specified. Training required 16 H200 GPUs—practical accessibility concerns not addressed.

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests provided. Some improvements are modest (60.9 vs. 57.7 on VSI-Bench average). Human performance on VSTI-Bench (77.0%) vs. model (58.8%) gap not deeply analyzed. Single training run reported; variance across random seeds unknown.

Limited analysis of why approach works: Insufficient investigation into what spatial relationships are captured. How much improvement comes from implicit 3D geometry vs. global metric scale? Why metric scale from CUT3R outperforms relative-scale VGGT? Missing qualitative examples and attention visualizations.

Data generation potential biases: Despite separate train/test splits, training data derived from same source datasets as evaluation. Automated QA generation could introduce systematic biases. Distribution shift from simulated route planning (Habitat) to real scenes not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important problem of extending VLMs to 3D spatial understanding from monocular video without depth sensors
Substantial dataset contributions: 200K+ spatial reasoning QA pairs and VSTI-Bench with 138.6K temporal reasoning samples
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, OST-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, Video-MME, VQAv2)
Achieves strong performance on VSI-Bench (rank 1 among open-source models) and competitive results on other spatial reasoning benchmarks
Includes ablation studies examining spatial tokens, view tokens, fusion strategies, and geometry encoder choices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: architecture reduces to frozen CUT3R + cross-attention + MLP fusion, which is incremental and standard
Critical missing ablation: no comparison of frozen vs. fine-tuned encoders despite freezing both visual and spatial modules

Evaluation restricted entirely to annotated synthetic scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes) with perfect ground-truth 3D annotations, severely limiting generalization claims to real-world scenarios
VSTI-Bench test set contains only ~6K samples, which is small for drawing strong conclusions; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported
Data curation lacks novelty: largely mirrors VSI-Bench [77] methodology and relies on existing Habitat simulator [59] without novel extensions

Questionable experimental design: inconsistent baseline comparisons (some fine-tuned on 200K data, others not), data leakage risk from overlapping datasets, and orthogonal mixed-domain training complicates interpretation
VSTI-Bench focuses narrowly on static scenes with camera motion only, excluding dynamic object motion and other spatio-temporal phenomena
Generalization evidence is weak: OpenEQA shows modest spatial gains (+1.65pp) with overall performance trade-off (-0.7pp); OST-Bench uses different baselines making comparisons unclear
Prohibitively high computational cost (16 H200 GPUs for 5 hours) and reliance on proprietary models (CUT3R, Qwen2, CLIP ViT) limit reproducibility
Misleading framing: title claims 'instruction-aligned 3D reconstruction' but method uses pre-computed frozen CUT3R features, not end-to-end learned reconstruction
Missing crucial ablations: no analysis of token resolution sensitivity, alternative fusion mechanisms beyond cross-attention, or comparative study of computational efficiency
No analysis of failure modes or error cases; limited investigation of robustness to CUT3R reconstruction errors that would occur in practice
Limited real-world validation: route planning task is benchmark-based, not actual navigation; no demonstrations on embodied AI or robotics applications despite problem motivation

strengths: Novel Spatial-Visual-View Fusion architecture that elegantly integrates metric-scale 3D reconstruction tokens from CUT3R with VLM representations via cross-attention
Principled technical approach: Metric-scale reconstruction (CUT3R) is well-justified over normalized approaches; ablation (Table D) clearly demonstrates superior performance on metric-dependent tasks
Comprehensive experimental validation across 7+ benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, Video-MME, OpenEQA) with consistent improvements
Substantial dataset contribution: 200K+ systematically generated spatial QA pairs with clear generation logic and well-designed spatio-temporal scene graphs
New benchmark contribution: VSTI-Bench with 138.6K temporal reasoning QA pairs addressing an identified gap in spatio-temporal evaluation
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, implementation specifics, hardware configuration, and training protocols enable reproduction
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, informative figures (particularly Figure 3), and comprehensive supplementary material
Practical design choices validated: Token-level fusion (60.90) outperforms explicit point cloud fusion (57.87), demonstrating sound engineering decisions
weaknesses: Significant domain limitation: All training and evaluation restricted to indoor static scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes). VSTI-Bench explicitly focuses on static scenes with camera-only motion, severely limiting applicability to outdoor/dynamic scenarios and generalization claims

Trade-offs with general video understanding: Video-MME degrades 62.7%→59.9% without mixing (-2.8pp); OpenEQA non-spatial drops 67.22%→65.54% (-1.68pp). While mixing helps, these trade-offs raise concerns for general-purpose deployment
Limited investigation of view tokens: View tokens (1×768) show largest ablation drop (60.90→59.09) but receive minimal analysis. No breakdown of task-type contributions or role characterization
VSTI-Bench quality concerns: Entirely automated generation without human validation; no inter-annotator agreement or difficulty assessment; route planning only 4,225 instances
Incomplete error analysis: No systematic failure case investigation or analysis of problematic spatial relationships. Task-wise analysis (Section C.1) is superficial
Missing computational cost analysis: CUT3R inference cost and failure modes not discussed, limiting practical understanding of deployment requirements
Statistical rigor absent: No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; no multi-run reporting or variance analysis
Early stopping after 1 epoch: No learning curves provided; unclear if longer training could improve results or if underfitting occurred
Potential data contamination not addressed: Unknown pre-training data for base model; possible overlap with CUT3R training data not discussed despite train/test split respect
Modest improvements in some settings: ScanQA only +1.8pp; Object Size metric slightly degrades (69.2 vs 70.8 baseline), suggesting benefits are task-dependent and not universal
